solutions.check: 32 entries verified against the grid (lengths, crossings, linked-clue mapping)

clue.text: Celeb wants sources of Viagra, extra fast!

indicators.note: a source is where something begins, so only the opening letters of the following words are used

blocks.note: a celebrity is a star
the opening letters of these two words

explanation.surface: A celebrity demands an urgent supply of Viagra, on the double.
explanation.walkthrough: 'fast!' reads as an adverb urging speed, but it is the verb meaning to go without food.
explanation.definitionFit: To fast is to go without eating, which is what one does when deprived of food entirely.

clue.text: "Making very fast progress is no possibility" (Corbyn's opening)

definitions.note: the answer is an adjective (at the speed of sound); the definition is a participial phrase

indicators.note: a possibility is one of several ways things could be arranged, so the letters may take a different order
an opening is where something starts, so only the first letter is used

blocks.note: taken as written
the first letter of the Labour leader's surname

explanation.surface: A quote, attributed to Jeremy Corbyn, claiming rapid progress is impossible.
explanation.walkthrough: Jeremy Corbyn was the Labour Party leader when this ran; only his initial is used.
explanation.definitionFit: Sonic speed is the speed of sound, a byword for travelling extremely quickly.

clue.text: A spider possibly could metamorphose into parrot? D'oh!

indicators.note: metamorphosis is a complete change of form, so the letters are reshaped into something new

blocks.note: taken as written
Homer Simpson's exclamation, taken as written without the apostrophe

explanation.surface: Someone wonders whether a spider might somehow turn into a parrot, then realises the stupidity.
explanation.walkthrough: Metamorphosis is a biology word, which fits the creatures in the scene while signalling a rearrangement.
explanation.definitionFit: Spiders belong to the invertebrate phylum with jointed legs and external skeletons; 'possibly' marks them as one example.

clue.text: see 12ac.
Gym exercises piss Ross off – "clubs should replace power"

indicators.note: to replace something is to put another thing in its place, so one letter swaps out for another
something that has gone off is spoiled, so these letters are no longer in their proper order

blocks.note: taken as written
C is the card-suit abbreviation for clubs
P is the physics symbol for power; this is the letter swapped out

explanation.surface: A command to annoy someone called Ross, with a political-sounding slogan about clubs and power.
explanation.walkthrough: First swap the P for C, giving CISSROSS, then rearrange. 'Piss off' is British slang for annoy or go away.
explanation.definitionFit: Scissor kicks and scissor jumps are standard workout moves in which the legs cross like blades.

clue.text: Stick to Dominic ultimately, not Remain!

indicators.note: ultimately means in the end, so only the final letter of the name is kept

blocks.note: the final letter of the name
in the Brexit referendum the alternative to Remain was Leave

explanation.surface: Advice to stay loyal to Dominic Cummings and back Brexit.
explanation.walkthrough: Dominic Cummings ran the Vote Leave campaign in the UK's 2016 EU referendum. The answer also means to split, but here it means to adhere.
explanation.definitionFit: This verb has two opposite senses; the older one is to adhere closely or remain faithful.

clue.text: Stretch top panties, extremely fancy, frantically removed by soldiers hoping for a bang

definitions.text: removed by soldiers hoping for a bang
definitions.note: a descriptive phrase standing for the plural noun

indicators.note: the top of a down word is its first letter, so only the opening is kept
the extremes of a word are its two ends, so only first and last letters are kept
frantic movement is wild and disordered, so the letters are thrown into a new order

blocks.note: the opening letter of this word
taken as written
the two end letters of this word

explanation.surface: Elastic-topped knickers are torn off in a hurry by squaddies hoping for sex.
explanation.walkthrough: 'A bang' looks like sex in this saucy surface, but it is a grenade going off: the pin must be pulled first.
explanation.definitionFit: A hand grenade has a pin that stops it detonating; a soldier pulls it out before throwing.

clue.text: Port – love it as liquid!

indicators.note: a liquid flows and takes any shape, so the letters run into a different arrangement

blocks.note: love is zero in tennis, which looks like the letter O
taken as written

explanation.surface: A wine lover says they enjoy port when it is drunk.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Port' suggests the fortified wine, a liquid, but it is a harbour town; 'as' belongs to the letters being rearranged.
explanation.definitionFit: Ostia was the ancient harbour city at the mouth of the Tiber serving Rome.

clue.text: A leek casually inserted during bonk – "get a move on!"

indicators.note: done casually means done carelessly, so the letters are not kept in their tidy order
to insert something during another thing is to put it in the middle, so one piece goes inside another

blocks.note: taken as written
both are British slang for having sex

explanation.surface: Someone casually slips a vegetable into proceedings during sex and urges haste.
explanation.walkthrough: The rearranged leek sits between the A and G of the four-letter slang word.
explanation.definitionFit: The idiom is an informal command telling someone to hurry up and stop dawdling.

clue.text: Head from Hugh Laurie's dodgy truck driver?

indicators.note: the head of a word is its first letter, so only that one is taken
dodgy means unreliable or crooked, so the letters are bent out of their order

blocks.note: the first letter of this name
taken as written

explanation.surface: Hugh Laurie's shady lorry driver is the subject of a question.
explanation.walkthrough: The 's in Laurie's is ignored. The question mark covers the definition: the word usually names a road-freight firm rather than a driver.
explanation.definitionFit: A haulier transports goods by road, so someone who drives freight lorries for a living fits loosely.

clue.text: No hint of actor screwing with Nate

indicators.note: screwing means twisting round, so the letters are twisted into a new order

blocks.note: taken as written
taken as written

explanation.surface: A gossip column denies any suggestion that an actor is sleeping with someone named Nate.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Screwing' is a sexual verb in the surface; in the wordplay it means twisting the letters.
explanation.definitionFit: Saying there is nothing at all, not the slightest sign, is the same as saying there is no hint.

clue.text: Gross Washington death sentence?

blocks.note: gross means obese
WA is the postal abbreviation for Washington state

explanation.surface: An outrageous capital sentence handed down in Washington.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Gross' looks like 'appalling', but it means fat. The question mark admits that not every one of these rulings condemns someone to death.
explanation.definitionFit: An Islamic legal ruling, famously the one issued against Salman Rushdie calling for his killing.

clue.text: (& 3dn.) In which one raised hand might represent thousands of "very into art deco" nuts

definitions.text: In which one raised hand might represent thousands

indicators.note: going into something means entering it, so one piece is placed inside another
nuts means crazy, so the letters go wild and are rearranged

blocks.note: v is the standard abbreviation for very
taken as written

explanation.surface: A description of some arty enthusiasts mad keen on 1920s design, with a raised hand.
explanation.walkthrough: At Labour and trade-union conferences a delegate holds up a card carrying the votes of thousands of members.
explanation.definitionFit: In this block system each delegate's raised card counts for the whole membership they represent.

clue.text: Labour deal which should quite rightly be abolished

definitions.text: Labour deal which should quite rightly be abolished

blocks.note: surface reading: an agreement struck by the Labour Party that critics want scrapped

blocks.clueFragment: Labour deal which should quite rightly be abolished
blocks.note: setter's reading: commerce in forced workers, which was outlawed in the nineteenth century

explanation.walkthrough: Capital L 'Labour' points to the political party; here it means toil, and the 'deal' is the buying and selling of people.
explanation.definitionFit: Traffic in human beings as forced workers is literally a business in labour, and it was abolished by law.

clue.text: Looking directly at organ, study with discretion

definitions.note: the answer is a noun phrase; the definition is a verb phrase describing the act

blocks.note: the eye is an organ of the body
to con is an old word for to study or learn by heart
tact is diplomatic discretion

explanation.surface: Someone stares at a body part and examines it discreetly, a cheeky Private Eye image.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Organ' hints at something rude, but it is simply the eye. Con meaning study is a crossword favourite from older English.
explanation.definitionFit: Meeting someone's gaze means two people looking straight into each other's eyes.

clue.text: (& 24ac.) PAYE hype: warn about rather optimistic message at this time?

definitions.text: rather optimistic message at this time?

indicators.note: about can mean turned around or scattered, so the letters are moved into a new order

blocks.note: Pay As You Earn, the British income-tax system, taken as written
taken as written
taken as written

explanation.surface: Commentary on tax-system hype, warning against a too-cheerful seasonal greeting.
explanation.walkthrough: PAYE is the UK system where tax is deducted from wages. The clue appeared around New Year, hence 'at this time'.
explanation.definitionFit: A seasonal greeting exchanged at the turn of January, called 'rather optimistic' given the gloomy news.

clue.text: Bottle each piss-poor sorrow

indicators.note: piss-poor means shoddily done, so the letters are badly ordered and need fixing

blocks.note: bottle is British slang for courage, as is heart
taken as written

explanation.surface: Each wretched bottle of drink brings misery.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Bottle' suggests drink; in British slang it means nerve or courage.
explanation.definitionFit: Emotional pain or grief, especially over love, is a deep and lasting sorrow.

clue.text: Request clumsy ape to get into lap dancing

indicators.note: clumsy movement is awkward and disordered, so the letters are jumbled
getting into something means entering it, so one piece goes inside another
dancing letters move about and change places

blocks.note: taken as written
taken as written

explanation.surface: A request for an awkward oaf to get into lap dancing.
explanation.walkthrough: Both three-letter words are rearranged; the first sits inside the second, between its P and L.
explanation.definitionFit: An appeal is an earnest plea or formal request for something.

clue.text: "Where the earth started moving on a big scale" – some dish, getting end away

indicators.note: sending the end away means its last letter is dropped

blocks.note: something epic is on a grand scale
an entrée is a dish served at a meal

explanation.surface: A saucy line about the earth moving during sex, plus an attractive person getting their end away.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Getting one's end away' is British slang for having sex; 'dish' suggests a sexy person. Here they cut the last E off a course of a meal.
explanation.definitionFit: The point on the surface directly above an earthquake's origin is where the ground shaking begins.

clue.text: Moreover, Dior creation depressed Marvin, for one

indicators.note: a creation is something newly made, so the letters are made into a new shape

blocks.note: and also means moreover
the fashion house's name, taken as written

explanation.surface: A Dior fashion design left someone called Marvin depressed.
explanation.walkthrough: Marvin the Paranoid Android is the gloomy robot in Douglas Adams's The Hitchhiker's Guide to the Galaxy.
explanation.definitionFit: Marvin is a famously miserable humanoid robot, which is what this science-fiction term means.

clue.text: Take pathetically bad union leader before court

indicators.note: done pathetically means done feebly and badly, so the letters are out of order
the leader of a word is its first letter, so only that is kept

blocks.note: taken as written
the first letter of this word
CT is the standard abbreviation for court

explanation.surface: A useless trade-union boss is hauled before the courts.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Union leader' reads as a trade-union chief, but it is just the first letter of union.
explanation.definitionFit: To take someone away by force or kidnap them is to carry them off illegally.

clue.text: Large body and rear ... gin-sozzled ... forever going on

indicators.note: sozzled means very drunk, so the letters stagger into a new order

blocks.note: the United Nations is a large international body
the rear is the back end
taken as written

explanation.surface: A fat drunk's backside and gin-soaked ramblings that never stop.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Large body' suggests an overweight person; it is the United Nations, a crossword staple.
explanation.definitionFit: Something that never stops or reaches a conclusion continues forever.

clue.text: Brothel madam protecting a female's name

indicators.note: to protect is to hold inside and shield, so the letters sit within the words around them

blocks.note: the letters run across the end of the first word and the start of the second

explanation.surface: A brothel keeper shields a woman's identity.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Protecting' suggests a madam guarding her workers, but it only signals letters held inside the phrase.
explanation.definitionFit: It is a woman's given name, as in the film Thelma and Louise.

clue.text: Desperately needing relief, snatched a drink of spirits

blocks.note: something snatched has been grabbed
a short is a small measure of spirits, as opposed to a long drink

explanation.surface: Someone desperate for comfort grabs a stiff drink.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Relief' reads as comfort, but the British idiom for being taken short means urgently needing a toilet.
explanation.definitionFit: The British idiom means suddenly needing to urinate or defecate with no lavatory close by.

clue.text: Writing stuff with protection of state – that's perverted

indicators.note: protection wraps around and encloses, so one piece is placed inside another

blocks.note: ink is the stuff you write with
KY is the postal abbreviation for Kentucky

explanation.surface: Writing material that enjoys state protection is called depraved.
explanation.walkthrough: The joke: KY is also a well-known brand of sexual lubricant, which suits a clue about perversion.
explanation.definitionFit: Kinky describes unconventional sexual tastes, the same as perverted in casual use.

clue.text: see 15ac.
(& 26dn.) Corrupt ruler and a member of the clergy

indicators.note: corrupt means spoiled or altered from its true form, so the letters are changed around

blocks.note: taken as written
taken as written

explanation.surface: A crooked monarch and a priest are in league together.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Corrupt ruler' looks like a crooked leader, but 'and a' joins the letters being rearranged too.
explanation.definitionFit: In the Church of England this priest supervises a group of parishes within a diocese.

clue.text: see 25dn.
Line dance scam – good one

blocks.note: a con is a scam
G is the abbreviation for good
a means one

explanation.surface: A dance craze is dismissed as a scam, but a nice one.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Good one' reads as praise, but it splits into two separate small pieces.
explanation.definitionFit: Dancers form a long snaking queue holding the hips of the person ahead, kicking out sideways.

clue.text: Labour leader has shameful secret, i.e. being a favourite of the Queen

indicators.note: a word's leader is its first letter, so only that is kept
something shameful is disgraceful and wrong, so the letters are put in disarray

blocks.note: the first letter of this word
taken as written

explanation.surface: The Labour leader hides a disgraceful secret: being a royal pet.
explanation.walkthrough: Robert Dudley, Earl of Leicester, was the favourite of Elizabeth I; 'the Queen' is not the modern monarch.
explanation.definitionFit: The Earl of Leicester was Elizabeth I's close companion and rumoured lover, her best-known courtier.

clue.text: Concerning the country's inept gay movement

definitions.note: an adjective meaning of a particular North African country

indicators.note: a movement shifts things from their places, so the letters are moved around

blocks.note: taken as written
taken as written

explanation.surface: A worry about a national gay-rights movement being badly run.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Movement' looks like a political campaign; it signals rearrangement. The definition is vague: 'the country' is the one the letters point to.
explanation.definitionFit: The adjective describes anything belonging to or relating to Egypt, a nation on the Nile.

clue.text: Bad example of international co-operation before Spring

blocks.note: the United Nations is an example of nations working together
a spring is a source of water, as is a well

explanation.surface: A poor showing of global cooperation ahead of the springtime season.
explanation.walkthrough: Capital S 'Spring' suggests the season, but it is a water source. 'Bad' here means feeling ill.
explanation.definitionFit: Feeling bad in the sense of being poorly or sick is the same as being ill.
